segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Finally then, brothers and sisters, we ask and urge you in the Lord Jesus that, just as you received from us how you must walk and please God—as indeed you are walking—you do so more and more.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this is God's will, your holiness: that you keep away from sexual immorality;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that each of you know how to gain control of your own body in holiness and honor,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: not in lustful passion like the Gentiles who do not know God;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that no one overstep the bounds and take advantage of a brother or sister in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, just as we told you before and solemnly warned you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God did not call us to impurity but in holiness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, whoever rejects this is rejecting not a human being but God, who indeed gives his Holy Spirit to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now about love for your brothers and sisters, you do not need anyone to write to you, for you yourselves are taught by God to love one another;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and indeed you are doing this toward all the brothers and sisters throughout Macedonia. But we urge you, brothers and sisters, to do so more and more,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to make it your ambition to live quietly, to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands, just as we instructed you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that you may walk decently toward outsiders and have need of no one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We do not want you to be uninformed, brothers and sisters, about those who are asleep, so that you will not grieve as the rest do, who have no hope.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if we believe that Jesus died and rose, then in the same way through Jesus God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this we tell you by a word of the Lord: we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will certainly not go ahead of those who have fallen asleep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the Lord himself, with a shout of command, with an archangel's voice and with God's trumpet, will come down from heaven, and the dead in Christ will rise first.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then we who are alive, who are left, will be snatched up together with them in clouds to meet the Lord in the air; and so we will always be with the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, encourage one another with these words.

notes.note: The Greek masculine plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group, and Paul is writing to the whole congregation. Many recent translations render it this way; others keep “brothers” and explain in a footnote. The singular in verse 6 is rendered “a brother or sister” on the same basis, though some interpreters think a male fellow believer is specifically in view there.

The word denotes being set apart for God and the way of life that follows from it. “Sanctification” has since become a technical term of theology, which the first readers would not have heard. “Holiness” also keeps visible the link Paul draws with the “Holy” Spirit in verse 8. Modern translations vary between the two.

notes.phrase: gain control of your own body
notes.note: The Greek is literally “acquire (or possess) his own vessel.” “Vessel” is a metaphor, and interpreters ancient and modern are divided on whether it means one's own body or one's wife. On the second reading the sense is “take a wife for himself in holiness and honor.” The verb normally means “acquire,” which favours “wife”; “vessel” as an image for the body is the better-attested usage. Most recent translations choose “body,” but the question remains open.

The same Greek word means “nations” or “peoples” and, in Jewish usage, the non-Jewish peoples in particular; this translation renders it by sense. Most of the Thessalonian believers were themselves non-Jews by birth. Paul nevertheless uses the word for outsiders who do not know God, placing his readers on the other side of that line.

notes.traditional: in any matter / in this matter
notes.note: The word can mean a business dealing, and some read the verse as a new topic: not cheating a fellow believer in commerce. The definite article and the surrounding verses on sexual conduct lead most scholars to take it as “the matter” under discussion, so that the wrong in view is sexual, such as adultery that violates another person's household.

notes.phrase: love for your brothers and sisters
notes.note: In ordinary Greek this word normally meant affection between actual siblings. Paul applies it to the members of the congregation, treating them as a family. The phrase “taught by God” translates a single compound word that is not found before Paul and may be his own coinage.

Sleep was a common euphemism for death in both Greek and Jewish usage, and the word alone does not settle any question about the state of the dead. Some translations render it plainly as “those who have died.” The metaphor is kept here because Paul uses the plain word “the dead” separately in verse 16.

notes.traditional: them also which sleep in Jesus
notes.note: In the Greek, “through Jesus” stands between “those who have fallen asleep” and “will bring,” and can attach to either. The older tradition reads “those who have fallen asleep through Jesus,” meaning those who died as his people. Many recent translations, as here, take it with the verb: God will bring them through Jesus' agency. Both readings have scholarly support.

notes.phrase: by a word of the Lord
notes.traditional: by the word of the Lord
notes.note: Paul claims the Lord's authority for what follows, but it is disputed what he means. He may mean a saying of Jesus handed down in the tradition, whether or not it is preserved in the Gospels. Or he may mean a revelation given through a Christian prophet, possibly Paul himself. The phrase echoes the Septuagint's language for prophetic messages.

The word means arrival and the presence that follows. In the period it was a regular term for the official visit of a king, emperor or high official to a city. Readers in a provincial city such as Thessalonica would have known that usage. Its sense is therefore fuller than the plain English “coming” suggests.

The verb means to seize or carry off suddenly and by force; it is used of robbers, wild animals and abductions. “Caught up” is accurate but has become mild with familiarity. The Latin translation of this word is the source of the English term “rapture.”

The Greek noun was often used for a city's delegation going out to welcome an arriving dignitary and escort him back in. Many scholars think Paul draws on that picture here, which would imply that those who meet the Lord accompany him on his arrival and are not taken away. Others doubt that the word is a technical term, and the text does not say what happens after the meeting.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed congregations recurs in every letter and translators split between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters”; the singular (v. 6) also needs a consistent policy.
The Semitic idiom for conduct recurs throughout Paul and John, and translations vary between “walk” and “live”; readers should see one choice.
Recurs across the Gospels, Acts, the letters and Revelation with renderings ranging from “fornication” to “sexual immorality” to “prostitution”; its scope needs one decision.
Translations alternate between “sanctification” and “holiness” across Romans, 1 Corinthians, the Thessalonian letters and Hebrews, and the choice should match the handling of ἅγιος and ἁγιάζω.
A very frequent verb whose senses (urge, appeal, encourage, comfort) need a fixed set of English renderings by sense to keep chapters consistent.
